items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An agreement in which member countries remove trade barriers among themselves but each keeps its own barriers against non-members"?
items.answer: free trade area
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of free trade area.

items.stem: Priya writes: "Brexit means the UK no longer trades freely with the EU at all." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (2021) keeps zero tariffs and quotas on goods meeting rules of origin, but the UK left the customs union and single market, so non-tariff barriers increased.
items.markingKey: The UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (2021) keeps zero tariffs and quotas on goods meeting rules of origin, but the UK left the customs union and single market, so non-tariff barriers increased. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that in a free trade area all members must charge the same tariff on imports from outside. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.

items.stem: Countries A, B and C form a free trade area. A has a 5% tariff on imported steel from outside, B has a 25% tariff. Explain why the FTA needs rules of origin, and why a customs union would not.
items.answer: Without rules of origin, outside steel would enter via A (5%) and move tariff-free to B (trade deflection). A customs union has a common external tariff, so the entry point does not matter.
items.markingKey: Without rules of origin, outside steel would enter via A (5%) and move tariff-free to B (trade deflection). A customs union has a common external tariff, so the entry point does not matter.

items.stem: Using the European single market as an example, explain a common market.
items.answer: Launched in 1993, the EU single market allows free movement of goods, services, capital and people among 27 member states (plus EEA members). Removing barriers to factor movements as well as goods deepened integration beyond a customs union
items.markingKey: Context (Launched in 1993, the EU single market allows free movement of goods, services, capital and people among 27 member states (plus EEA members).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Removing barriers to factor movements as well as goods deepened integration beyond a customs union – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a common market.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that regional trading blocs are a stepping stone towards global free trade.
items.answer: Blocs can be building blocks if open and WTO-consistent, but proliferation of overlapping agreements and diversion may also make them stumbling blocks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: liberalise trade among many countries; deeper integration than WTO rules (services, standards); build institutions and support for openness. Arguments against: trade diversion harms outsiders; complex "spaghetti bowl" of rules of origin; reduce interest in multilateral negotiations; can become rival blocs. Supported judgement: Blocs can be building blocks if open and WTO-consistent, but proliferation of overlapping agreements and diversion may also make them stumbling blocks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "bilateral trade agreement"?
options: The replacement of lower-cost imports from a non-member by higher-cost imports from a member of a trading bloc, because of the common external tariff
A trade agreement between two countries
An agreement in which member countries remove trade barriers among themselves but each keeps its own barriers against non-members
A single tariff imposed by all members of a customs union on imports from non-members
items.answer: A trade agreement between two countries
items.markingKey: B. "bilateral trade agreement" is a trade agreement between two countries.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a customs union and a free trade area.
items.answer: In a free trade area members remove barriers among themselves but keep their own external tariffs; a customs union also adopts a common external tariff and usually negotiates trade as a bloc.

items.stem: Using Estonia's adoption of the euro in 2011 as an example, explain one monetary policy for different economies.
items.answer: Estonia joined the euro in 2011 despite the recent crisis and later experienced inflation above 20% in 2022, the highest in the euro area. The ECB's interest rate was set for the whole area and was too low for Estonia's overheating economy

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The benefits of the euro have outweighed its costs for member countries."
items.answer: Benefits have been greater for open, well-synchronised economies; for periphery economies costs were large during crises, so the outcome depends on convergence and on fiscal and banking union.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower transaction costs and exchange risk; price transparency and competition; low inflation and credibility for previously high-inflation members; deeper capital markets. Arguments against: loss of independent monetary policy and exchange-rate adjustment; asymmetric shocks and the 2010-2012 crisis; limited fiscal transfers and labour mobility; divergence between core and periphery. Supported judgement: Benefits have been greater for open, well-synchronised economies; for periphery economies costs were large during crises, so the outcome depends on convergence and on fiscal and banking union.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "monetary union"?

The central bank of the eurozone, which sets the single interest rate for all member countries with a mandate of price stability (2% inflation)
A group of countries that share a single currency and a single central bank with one monetary policy
Immediate effects on resource allocation, such as trade creation and trade diversion
items.answer: A group of countries that share a single currency and a single central bank with one monetary policy
items.markingKey: C. "monetary union" is a group of countries that share a single currency and a single central bank with one monetary policy.

items.stem: Explain why a member of a monetary union may find it harder to recover from a recession.
items.answer: It cannot cut its own interest rates or devalue its currency; it must rely on fiscal policy (limited by deficit rules) or falling wages and prices (internal devaluation), which is slow and painful.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It cannot cut its own interest rates or devalue its currency; it must rely on fiscal policy (limited by deficit rules) or falling wages and prices (internal devaluation), which is slow and painful. items.answer: Trade creation replaces higher-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from a partner, raising efficiency; trade diversion replaces lower-cost non-member imports with higher-cost partner imports, reducing efficiency.

items.stem: Lumeria can produce tablet computers domestically at $107 each. Zedland can supply them at $67 and Sundara at $63 (the lowest-cost producer). Lumeria charges a tariff of 80% on all imports. Lumeria then forms a customs union with Zedland, removing the tariff on imports from Zedland but keeping it on Sundara. Determine where Lumeria buys tablet computers before and after the customs union, and state whether this is trade creation or trade diversion.
items.answer: Before: domestic $107 < Zedland $121 and Sundara $113 with tariff, so Lumeria produces domestically. After: Zedland sells at $67 < $107, so Lumeria imports from Zedland – trade creation (higher-cost domestic output replaced by lower-cost imports).
items.markingKey: [M1] tariff-inclusive prices: Sundara $113, Zedland $121; [A1] source before; [A1] source after; [R1] correct classification. Before: domestic $107 < Zedland $121 and Sundara $113 with tariff, so Lumeria produces domestically. After: Zedland sells at $67 < $107, so Lumeria imports from Zedland – trade creation (higher-cost domestic output replaced by lower-cost imports).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that customs unions generally create more trade than they divert.
items.answer: The balance depends on the height of the common external tariff and on whether members are already efficient producers; dynamic gains often matter more than static effects.

items.answer: The ASEAN Free Trade Area has reduced tariffs on almost all intra-ASEAN trade to 0-5% for its ten members. Members liberalised trade among themselves while keeping separate external tariffs

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Joining a monetary union guarantees that inflation will be the same in every member country." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: There is one policy rate, but inflation differs because of different growth, wage settlements, energy mixes and tax changes (e.g. 2022: France about 6% vs Estonia over 20%).
items.markingKey: There is one policy rate, but inflation differs because of different growth, wage settlements, energy mixes and tax changes (e.g. 2022: France about 6% vs Estonia over 20%). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the European single market shows a common market.
items.answer: Launched in 1993, the EU single market allows free movement of goods, services, capital and people among 27 member states (plus EEA members). Removing barriers to factor movements as well as goods deepened integration beyond a customs union
items.markingKey: Context (Launched in 1993, the EU single market allows free movement of goods, services, capital and people among 27 member states (plus EEA members).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Removing barriers to factor movements as well as goods deepened integration beyond a customs union – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a common market.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the euro-area sovereign debt crisis shows disadvantages of monetary union.
items.answer: Between 2010 and 2012 Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus needed financial assistance; without their own currencies they could not devalue and had to cut wages and spending. Asymmetric shocks and the loss of independent monetary and exchange-rate policy forced painful internal devaluation
items.markingKey: Context (Between 2010 and 2012 Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus needed financial assistance; without their own currencies they could not devalue and had to cut wages and spending.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Asymmetric shocks and the loss of independent monetary and exchange-rate policy forced painful internal devaluation – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to disadvantages of monetary union.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Mercosur and Brazilian car trade shows trade creation and diversion.
items.answer: After Mercosur was formed, Argentina's imports of cars and parts shifted strongly towards Brazil. Some trade replaced costly domestic production (creation), while some replaced cheaper imports from outside the bloc (diversion)
items.markingKey: Context (After Mercosur was formed, Argentina's imports of cars and parts shifted strongly towards Brazil.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Some trade replaced costly domestic production (creation), while some replaced cheaper imports from outside the bloc (diversion) – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to trade creation and diversion.

items.stem: A student claims that brexit means the UK no longer trades freely with the EU at all. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (2021) keeps zero tariffs and quotas on goods meeting rules of origin, but the UK left the customs union and single market, so non-tariff barriers increased.
items.markingKey: The UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (2021) keeps zero tariffs and quotas on goods meeting rules of origin, but the UK left the customs union and single market, so non-tariff barriers increased. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the benefits of the euro have outweighed its costs for member countries.
items.answer: Benefits have been greater for open, well-synchronised economies; for periphery economies costs were large during crises, so the outcome depends on convergence and on fiscal and banking union.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower transaction costs and exchange risk; price transparency and competition; low inflation and credibility for previously high-inflation members; deeper capital markets. Arguments against: loss of independent monetary policy and exchange-rate adjustment; asymmetric shocks and the 2010-2012 crisis; limited fiscal transfers and labour mobility; divergence between core and periphery. Supported judgement: Benefits have been greater for open, well-synchronised economies; for periphery economies costs were large during crises, so the outcome depends on convergence and on fiscal and banking union.

items.stem: You are an analyst at a regional development bank. A minister argues that customs unions generally create more trade than they divert. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: The balance depends on the height of the common external tariff and on whether members are already efficient producers; dynamic gains often matter more than static effects.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: members are often natural trading partners; dynamic gains: economies of scale, competition, FDI; evidence from the EU single market. Counter-points: high external tariffs encourage diversion; outsiders lose market access; CAP-type policies divert agricultural trade. Recommendation: The balance depends on the height of the common external tariff and on whether members are already efficient producers; dynamic gains often matter more than static effects. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "customs union".
items.answer: A free trade area in which members also adopt a common external tariff against non-members
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a free trade area in which members also adopt a common external tariff against non-members. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of monetary union?
items.answer: Loss of independent monetary policy
items.markingKey: C. One interest rate for all members.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "trade diversion".
items.answer: The replacement of lower-cost imports from a non-member by higher-cost imports from a member of a trading bloc, because of the common external tariff
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the replacement of lower-cost imports from a non-member by higher-cost imports from a member of a trading bloc, because of the common external tariff. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a free trade area and a customs union.
items.answer: In a free trade area members remove barriers among themselves but keep their own external tariffs; a customs union also adopts a common external tariff and usually negotiates trade as a bloc.
items.markingKey: In a free trade area members remove barriers among themselves but keep their own external tariffs; a customs union also adopts a common external tariff and usually negotiates trade as a bloc. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a single currency can increase trade among member countries.
items.answer: It removes currency conversion costs and exchange-rate uncertainty, and makes prices transparent, encouraging cross-border trade and investment.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It removes currency conversion costs and exchange-rate uncertainty, and makes prices transparent, encouraging cross-border trade and investment. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that trade diversion is good for the importing country because it pays a lower price than before. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Consumers may pay slightly less, but the government loses tariff revenue and resources are used less efficiently, so national welfare can fall.
items.markingKey: Consumers may pay slightly less, but the government loses tariff revenue and resources are used less efficiently, so national welfare can fall. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why trading blocs may conflict with the aims of the WTO.
items.answer: They discriminate against non-members, breaking the most-favoured-nation principle and possibly diverting trade from more efficient outside producers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They discriminate against non-members, breaking the most-favoured-nation principle and possibly diverting trade from more efficient outside producers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Priya writes: "In a monetary union each country's central bank chooses its own interest rate." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: There is one interest rate set by a single central bank (the ECB) for all members.
items.markingKey: There is one interest rate set by a single central bank (the ECB) for all members. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between trade creation and trade diversion.
items.answer: Trade creation replaces higher-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from a partner, raising efficiency; trade diversion replaces lower-cost non-member imports with higher-cost partner imports, reducing efficiency.
items.markingKey: Trade creation replaces higher-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from a partner, raising efficiency; trade diversion replaces lower-cost non-member imports with higher-cost partner imports, reducing efficiency. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the UK joining the EEC in 1973 and explain what it reveals about trade diversion.
items.answer: When the UK joined the EEC, it adopted the Common External Tariff, and imports of food such as butter and lamb shifted from New Zealand and Australia towards European producers. Lower-cost Commonwealth suppliers were replaced by higher-cost European producers protected by the common tariff and CAP

items.stem: Using the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) as an example, explain forms of economic integration.
